bib.title: Knowledge graphs and LLMs: A killer combination (Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action, ch. 1)

question: Why combine knowledge graphs and LLMs, and what is a knowledge graph?
hypothesis: KGs and LLMs overcome each other's limitations: LLMs build and query KGs, KGs ground LLMs.
contributions: A new definition of a knowledge graph with four pillars (evolution, semantics, integration, learning)
Checklist for deciding whether a KG and/or an LLM is needed
Comparison of RDF and labeled property graphs

results.claim: A KG is defined as an ever-evolving graph of typed entities, attributes and named relationships, built for a domain, integrating structured and unstructured data.
results.setup: Chapter 1 of Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action (Manning); conceptual introduction, no experiments
results.quote: A knowledge graph is an ever-evolving graph data structure composed of a set of typed entities, their attributes, and meaningful named relationships.

results.claim: McKinsey estimate: addressing data fragmentation can cut annual data spending by 5% to 15% in the short term.
results.source: McKinsey & Company [12] (reference list not in the extracted chapter)
results.setup: Chapter 1 of Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action (Manning); conceptual introduction, no experiments; cited from McKinsey & Company [12], not measured for KGs
results.quote: addressing data fragmentation can cut annual data spending by 5% to 15% in the short term

results.claim: KGs mitigate LLM hallucination, stale information and lack of explainability.
results.setup: Chapter 1 of Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action (Manning); conceptual introduction, no experiments; cites [10]
results.quote: Hallucinations—KGs provide structured, verified knowledge that acts as a factual foundation

results.claim: KGs have not been widely adopted because they are costly to build, need multi-hop access patterns, and scatter results across nodes.
results.setup: Chapter 1 of Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action (Manning); conceptual introduction, no experiments
results.quote: They are expensive to build and maintain in terms of time, effort, and money.

results.claim: RDF excels at interoperability and semantic consistency; LPG at pathfinding and traversal.
results.setup: Chapter 1 of Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action (Manning); conceptual introduction, no experiments
results.quote: LPG implementations provide advantages in pathfinding queries and graph traversal operations.

results.claim: Modern KGs adopt 'just enough semantics': a subset of ontology features, partial ontologies extended organically.
results.setup: Chapter 1 of Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action (Manning); conceptual introduction, no experiments
results.quote: Modern KGs adopt a pragmatic approach characterized by “just enough semantics.”

results.claim: Consider LLMs if even one of four needs applies (extract from text, interpret queries, conversational interface, summarise).
results.setup: Chapter 1 of Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action (Manning); conceptual introduction, no experiments
results.quote: If you answer yes to even one of these, you need LLMs to empower your KG-based solution.

limits: No experiments or measured results; claims are assertions or cited from other work
Reference list is not in the extracted chapter, so citations [1]-[15] cannot be resolved
Figures 1.1-1.6 carry content not in the text layer
practices: Start from the business need, then data, then algorithms (1.7).
Use the yes/no checklists to decide whether a KG and an LLM are needed (1.5.3).
Adopt just enough semantics: partial ontologies scoped to a subdomain, extended as needed (1.6.1).
Use LLMs for entity/relation extraction, querying (text-to-Cypher) and summarising (1.3).

terms.definition: an ever-evolving graph data structure composed of a set of typed entities, their attributes, and meaningful named relationships. Built for a specific domain, it integrates both structured and unstructured data to craft knowledge for humans and machines
a PLM with significant scale—typically tens or hundreds of billions of parameters
prioritizes data engineering to improve both the quality and quantity of data used for training high-complexity ML models
represent the hierarchical dimension of the data, organizing categories in broader–narrower relationships
introduce more complex relationships beyond simple hierarchies: identity, difference, class definitions incl. union, complement, disjointness, cardinality
a data model that focuses on knowledge representation, where the graph is encoded as a collection of statements or triplets
representation focuses on the structure (properties and relationships) of the graph; nodes and edges have properties
